response_text:
## 18-Month Savings Outcome

With a **$6,000** deposit left untouched for **18 months**, **Account Y** gives the highest ending balance.

Media: Icon=https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/bootstrap-icons@1.11.3/icons/currency-dollar.svg

- **Best ending balance:** Account Y
- **Best no-fee simplicity:** Account X
- **Best flexibility:** Account Z

## Ending Balance Comparison

Using the stated APY-style nominal rates and compounding schedules:

| Account | Rate | Compounding | Fees Applied | Estimated Ending Balance | Net Gain |
|---|---:|---|---|---:|---:|
| X | 4.1% | Monthly | $0 | **$6,377.74** | **$377.74** |
| Y | 4.4% | Daily | $0 at $6,000 balance | **$6,411.29** | **$411.29** |
| Z | 3.8% | Monthly | $0 | **$6,347.84** | **$347.84** |

**Winner: Account Y**, by about:
- **$33.55** more than Account X
- **$63.45** more than Account Z

## What Matters Beyond the Raw Total

### Account Y: highest return
Media: Icon=https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/bootstrap-icons@1.11.3/icons/star.svg
- Best choice if your priority is **maximum balance after 18 months**.
- The **$5 monthly fee is waived** because your deposit is **above $5,000**.
- Tradeoff: if your balance drops below the waiver threshold later, fees could reduce its advantage.

### Account X: strongest simple alternative
Media: Icon=https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/bootstrap-icons@1.11.3/icons/piggy-bank.svg
- Very close to Y in outcome.
- No fees and only a **$1,000 minimum**, so it is easier to keep long term.
- Good pick if you want **predictability without monitoring balance thresholds**.

### Account Z: best liquidity, weakest return
Media: Icon=https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/bootstrap-icons@1.11.3/icons-arrow-left-right.svg
- Lowest ending balance here.
- Main advantage is **unlimited withdrawals**.
- Best only if access flexibility matters more than earning the last extra dollars.

## Decision Lens for Your Goal

If your goal is strictly **“deposit $6,000 and do not touch it for 18 months,”** choose **Account Y**.

If you want the best balance with the least chance of fee surprises:
- **Choose X** if you might let the balance dip below $5,000 later.
- **Choose Z** only if you highly value withdrawal flexibility.

## Calculation Context

I treated the quoted rates as nominal annual rates with the stated compounding frequency.

Formula:
- Monthly compounding: \( A = P\left(1+\frac{r}{12}\right)^{18} \)
- Daily compounding: \( A = P\left(1+\frac{r}{365}\right)^{365 \cdot 1.5} \)

Where:
- \( P = 6000 \)
- \( r \) is the annual rate
- Time = **1.5 years**

## Quick Actions

Action: [Button: Recheck math] https://www.calculator.net/interest-calculator.html
Action: [Button: Compare APY] https://www.investor.gov/financial-tools-calculators/calculators/compound-interest-calculator

## Sources

- Compound interest reference: <https://www.investor.gov/financial-tools-calculators/calculators/compound-interest-calculator>
- Interest calculator: <https://www.calculator.net/interest-calculator.html>

response_text:
## 2016 Civic Charging-System Snapshot
Most likely, this is a **belt/charging-system wear issue**, not an immediate no-start emergency. The pattern of **brief cold-start squeal + slight dimming at idle with AC load + reliable starts + no warning lights** points first to a **worn or slipping serpentine belt**, with **battery aging** and **marginal charging at idle** as secondary possibilities.

Media: Icon=https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/bootstrap-icons@1.11.3/icons/car-front.svg

### Likely causes, in order
- **Serpentine belt wear or slip** — most likely cause of a few seconds of squeal on startup, especially with accessory load.
- **Weak belt tensioner or pulley bearing** — can allow belt slip or brief noise when cold.
- **Battery aging** — at **4 years old**, it may still work fine in a warm climate, but slight voltage sag at idle becomes more noticeable.
- **Alternator output weak at idle** — possible, but less likely than belt/tensioner if there are no warning lights and starts remain strong.
- **Normal idle dimming under AC load** — slight dimming can be normal, but paired with squeal it deserves a quick check.

## First Checks to Do at Home or at a Parts Store
| Step | Action | What to Check | Expected Result |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Inspect serpentine belt | Cracks, glazing, frayed edges, shiny ribs | Belt should look dry, even, and not polished |
| 2 | Listen at cold start | Squeal duration and whether AC on/off changes it | Brief squeal suggests belt slip or tension issue |
| 3 | Check battery age/terminals | Corrosion, loose clamps, case swelling | Clean, tight terminals; no swelling |
| 4 | Get free battery/charging test | Battery voltage, cranking health, alternator output | Battery and charging should both pass |
| 5 | Observe headlights at idle | Compare AC off vs AC on vs slight rev to 1,500 rpm | Dimming that improves with revs suggests low idle output/load issue |
| 6 | Inspect tensioner/pulleys | Vibration, wobble, chirp, rough spin noise | Smooth operation, no wobble or bearing noise |

## Under-$400 Repair Priorities
### Fix soon
- **Serpentine belt**
  Usually the best first spend if the belt is old or glazed. Often relatively inexpensive and strongly matches your cold-start squeal.
- **Belt tensioner**
  Fix soon if the belt looks okay but squeal persists, or if the tensioner/pulley shows wobble or noise.
- **Battery replacement**
  Worth doing soon **only if it tests weak**. In a warm climate, 4 years is not automatically end-of-life, but it is in the watch zone.

### Okay to monitor for now
- **Very slight headlight dimming at idle with AC on**
  Often acceptable if:
  - starting remains strong
  - battery/charging test passes
  - dimming is minor
  - no battery/charging warning light appears
- **No-warning-light, no-starting-problem condition**
  If all tests pass, this does not sound like a high-risk immediate failure today.

### Escalate sooner if any of these start happening
- Squeal lasts longer or happens warm, not just on cold starts
- Battery light comes on
- Slow cranking starts
- Lights dim heavily or blower speed drops at idle
- Burning rubber smell
- Repeated chirping/grinding from pulley area

## Best Budget Plan for Your Situation
Given your **under-$400** limit, this is the smartest order:

Option 1: **Test first, then replace belt if worn** | Best value if squeal is brief and startup remains reliable | Usually most likely fix
Action: [Button: Find Honda Service] https://automobiles.honda.com/tools/dealer-locator

Option 2: **Battery/alternator test at a parts store** | Usually free and helps avoid unnecessary replacement | Best diagnostic starting point
Action: [Button: Free Battery Test] https://www.autozone.com/lp/free-battery-charging-system-testing

Option 3: **Replace belt + tensioner only if inspection supports it** | Good if squeal continues after belt inspection or belt condition is borderline | May still fit under budget at an independent shop
Action: [Button: Get Repair Estimate] https://repairpal.com/estimator

### Practical recommendation
- **Do first this week:** free **battery/charging test** + **belt inspection**
- **Most likely repair under budget:** **serpentine belt replacement**
- **Next most likely add-on:** **tensioner/pulley**
- **Do not replace the battery blindly** unless it tests weak

## Useful Context for This Recommendation
- Warm climate helps battery life somewhat, but **4 years old** still puts it in a reasonable test/recheck window.
- Your daily driving of **25 miles/day** is enough that chronic undercharging is less likely than with very short-trip driving.
- No warning lights and reliable starts lower the odds of a major alternator failure right now.

## Quick Actions
Action: [Button: Find Test Location] https://www.oreillyauto.com/store-services/free-battery-testing
Action: [Button: Estimate Costs] https://repairpal.com/estimator

## Sources
- Honda owner resources: <https://owners.honda.com/>
- AutoZone free battery and charging tests: <https://www.autozone.com/lp/free-battery-charging-system-testing>
- RepairPal estimator: <https://repairpal.com/estimator>

## Junior Data Analyst Fit for Berlin Role

For this role, **Candidate A is the better fit** because the job emphasizes **stakeholder communication, weekly reporting, and quick ramp-up**. A’s stronger reporting-tool experience and longer practical exposure align more directly with immediate business needs.

## Side-by-Side Candidate Comparison

| Candidate | Relevant Strengths | Likely Gaps | Fit for This Role | Ramp-Up Outlook |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Candidate A | 1.5 years internship experience; strong SQL and Excel; Power BI dashboards; business degree | Beginner Python; may be lighter on statistical depth | **Best overall fit** for reporting-heavy, stakeholder-facing work | **Fastest** |
| Candidate B | Strong Python and pandas; decent SQL; statistics degree | Only 6 months internship; no dashboard tools; less evidence of business-facing reporting | Better for a more technical or analytics-heavy junior path | Moderate |

### Best-Fit Recommendation

**Choose Candidate A** if the hiring priority is:
- owning weekly reporting quickly
- working with business stakeholders
- producing dashboards and recurring insights with minimal onboarding

**Choose Candidate B** only if the team can tolerate a slower business ramp-up in exchange for stronger longer-term coding/statistics upside.

## Hiring Risks to Watch

### Candidate A risks
Media: Icon=https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/bootstrap-icons@1.11.3/icons/person-workspace.svg
- **Python ceiling:** may struggle if the role expands beyond reporting into automation or deeper analysis.
- **Analytical depth:** business degree plus beginner Python may indicate more BI/reporting strength than rigorous analytical problem-solving.
- **Tool dependency:** may rely heavily on SQL/Excel/Power BI workflows rather than scalable scripting.

### Candidate B risks
Media: Icon=https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/bootstrap-icons@1.11.3/icons/person-workspace.svg
- **Slow reporting ramp-up:** no dashboard tooling experience is a direct risk for weekly reporting ownership.
- **Stakeholder readiness:** less internship time means less evidence of managing ambiguous business requests.
- **Business translation gap:** may be technically capable but weaker at turning analysis into simple business updates.

## Interview Questions That Will Validate the Decision

### Questions for both candidates
- Describe a weekly or recurring report you owned. What was the audience, what inputs did you use, and how did you ensure accuracy?
- Tell me about a time a stakeholder asked for something unclear. How did you clarify the request and deliver the right output?
- If a KPI suddenly drops week over week, how would you investigate it in your first hour?
- How do you check data quality before sending a report to leadership?
- Explain one project where your analysis changed a business decision.

### Extra questions for Candidate A
- Walk through a Power BI dashboard you built: audience, metrics, refresh process, and decisions it supported.
- Show how you would use Python to automate part of a recurring reporting workflow.
- When would Excel be enough, and when would you move the work into SQL or Python?

### Extra questions for Candidate B
- How would you build a stakeholder-friendly weekly report if you had only SQL, Python, and spreadsheets available?
- Describe how you would structure a dashboard for non-technical business users, even if you have not built one before.
- Give an example of simplifying a statistical finding for a manager with no analytics background.

## Decision Lens for Final Round

Use a simple scorecard weighted to the actual role needs:
- **Stakeholder communication:** 35%
- **Weekly reporting ownership:** 30%

response_text:
# Sales Performance Snapshot

Using the 6-month dataset, the biggest story is **steady growth with one clear dip in April**. Revenue rises from **42,000 to 56,000** overall, while website visits and conversion rate also improve by June, suggesting the sales engine is getting more efficient after a short disruption.

**Top KPI highlights**
- **Revenue:** up **33.3%** from Jan to Jun
- **Ad spend:** up **33.3%** from Jan to Jun
- **Website visits:** up **36.1%** from Jan to Jun
- **Conversion rate:** up from **2.1% to 2.4%**
- **Month needing investigation:** **2026-04**

# Metrics That Matter Most

| Month | Revenue | Ad Spend | Website Visits | Conversion Rate | ROAS | Revenue per Visit |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 2026-01 | 42,000 | 6,000 | 18,000 | 2.1% | 7.00x | 2.33 |
| 2026-02 | 45,000 | 6,500 | 19,500 | 2.0% | 6.92x | 2.31 |
| 2026-03 | 47,000 | 7,200 | 21,000 | 2.2% | 6.53x | 2.24 |
| 2026-04 | 43,000 | 7,000 | 20,500 | 1.8% | 6.14x | 2.10 |
| 2026-05 | 52,000 | 7,600 | 23,000 | 2.3% | 6.84x | 2.26 |
| 2026-06 | 56,000 | 8,000 | 24,500 | 2.4% | 7.00x | 2.29 |

### Key trends
- **Overall growth is healthy.** Revenue, traffic, and conversion all end higher than where they started.
- **April breaks the pattern.** Revenue falls from **47,000 to 43,000** despite only a small drop in visits and ad spend remaining high.
- **Conversion rate explains most of the April weakness.** It drops to **1.8%**, the lowest point in the dataset.
- **Recovery is strong in May and June.** Revenue jumps sharply as both visits and conversion improve.
- **Marketing efficiency is fairly stable.** ROAS stays in a fairly tight range, but April is the weakest month.

### What likely matters most
- **Conversion rate is the most sensitive driver** here. Traffic grows fairly steadily, but the biggest revenue swing happens when conversion rate dips.
- **Traffic quality appears mostly good.** When visits rise and conversion holds up, revenue responds quickly.
- **Ad spend alone is not the growth story.** Spend rises gradually, but revenue performance improves most when conversion and visits improve together.

# Best Charts to Build

Option 1: Revenue + Ad Spend dual-axis line chart | Shows whether revenue growth is keeping pace with marketing investment | Best for efficiency trend
Action: [Button: Build Chart] https://www.google.com/sheets/about/

Option 2: Website Visits and Conversion Rate combo chart | Reveals whether traffic growth is translating into buyer action | Best for diagnosing funnel health
Action: [Button: Build Chart] https://support.google.com/docs/answer/9142829

Option 3: Monthly ROAS bar chart | Makes underperforming months immediately visible, especially April | Best for executive review
Action: [Button: Build Chart] https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/power-bi/visuals/power-bi-visualization-combo-chart

# April Investigation Focus

Media: Icon=https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/bootstrap-icons@1.11.3/icons/search.svg

**2026-04 deserves investigation** because several signals weaken at once:
- Revenue drops **8.5%** vs March
- Conversion rate falls from **2.2% to 1.8%**
- Visits slip only slightly, so the issue is probably **not just traffic volume**
- ROAS falls to **6.14x**, the lowest month

### Likely causes to check
- Landing page or checkout friction
- Lower-quality traffic from a campaign mix change
- Product stock, pricing, or promotion changes
- Tracking error in conversion measurement
- Seasonal demand softness specific to April

# Quick Actions

Action: [Button: Plot in Sheets] https://www.google.com/sheets/about/
Action: [Button: Use Power BI] https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/power-platform/products/power-bi

# Sources

- Microsoft Power BI combo charts: <https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/power-bi/visuals/power-bi-visualization-combo-chart>

response_text:
## Melbourne Rental Fit for a 3-Day CBD Commute

For a new job starting in **2026-02**, all three options fit the stated budget and commute limit. The best overall fit is **South Yarra** if commute ease and workday convenience matter most, while **Footscray** is the best value pick.

## Ranked Rental Comparison

| Rank | Option | Weekly Rent | CBD Commute | Fit for Remote Work | Laundry / Layout | Main Tradeoff |
|---|---|---:|---:|---|---|---|
| 1 | **B. South Yarra** | **AUD 640** | **22 min** | Good, likely quieter in a modern build if not on a main road | 1 bed, smaller, modern | Highest rent; less space; no parking |
| 2 | **A. Footscray** | **AUD 520** | **38 min** | Fair to good, larger space helps create a work zone | 1 bed, larger, older building | Longer commute; building age may affect noise/insulation |
| 3 | **C. Coburg** | **AUD 610** | **44 min** | Good natural light helps for WFH | 2 bed, older kitchen | Right near the commute limit; paying for extra bedroom you did not ask for |

### 1) South Yarra — Best overall balance
Option 1: **South Yarra** | Best mix of short commute, modern condition, and likely lower day-to-day friction for a CBD worker | **22-minute commute**
Media: Icon=https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/bootstrap-icons@1.11.3/icons/building.svg
- Strongest fit for commuting **3 days a week**: the short trip reduces fatigue and makes early starts, late finishes, and social/work events easier.
- Modern buildings often mean better thermal comfort, newer appliances, and a cleaner WFH setup.
- It uses almost the full budget, so your flexibility for rent increases or utilities is lower.
- The smaller footprint is the biggest downside if you need a clearly separated desk area.
- No parking is not a major negative unless you already own a car.

**Why it ranks first:** your commute constraint is important and recurring, and this option gives the biggest quality-of-life benefit every week without breaking budget.

### 2) Footscray — Best value
Option 2: **Footscray** | Lowest rent with more space, making it easier to work from home comfortably | **AUD 520/week**
Media: Icon=https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/bootstrap-icons@1.11.3/icons/currency-dollar.svg
- Best price by a clear margin, leaving about **AUD 130/week** versus your max budget.
- Larger space is useful for remote work, especially if you want a desk away from the bed/living area.
- A **38-minute commute** is still acceptable for 3 days a week.
- The older building is the main risk: noise insulation, heating/cooling efficiency, and laundry quality may be less reliable depending on the exact apartment.
- If “quiet enough for remote work” is a top priority, building condition and street exposure matter more here than in South Yarra.

**Why it ranks second:** best affordability and space, but with more uncertainty around comfort and noise.

### 3) Coburg — Space-heavy, but less aligned to your brief
Option 3: **Coburg** | Extra room and good light, but closest to missing your commute target and not optimized for a 1-bedroom brief | **44-minute commute**
Media: Icon=https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/bootstrap-icons@1.11.3/icons/house.svg
- The second bedroom could be excellent as a dedicated office, which is a real advantage for remote work.
- Good natural light is a meaningful plus if you spend long hours at home.
- At **44 minutes**, it barely stays within your door-to-door limit; any transfer friction or service disruption could push it over.
- You would be paying for space you did not explicitly need.
- The older kitchen is mostly a lifestyle issue, but it may signal broader apartment age/maintenance tradeoffs.

**Why it ranks third:** good home-working potential, but weaker fit on commute reliability and requirement match.

## Best Choice by Priority

- **Best overall:** **South Yarra**
  - Choose this if you want the smoothest weekly routine and least commute burden.
- **Best value:** **Footscray**
  - Choose this if keeping costs down and having more room matters more than saving commute time.
- **Best WFH layout potential:** **Coburg**
  - Choose this only if a separate office area is worth accepting a near-limit commute.

## Practical Decision Notes for February 2026

Working in the CBD **3 days per week** usually makes commute quality a major factor, but not the only one. Because you also need a place quiet enough for remote work, the ranking depends on how you weight **time vs space vs building quality**:

- If you expect frequent office days, networking, or late finishes, **South Yarra** is the safest choice.
- If you want to optimize total living value and monthly cash flow, **Footscray** is the smartest budget-conscious option.
- If remote work setup matters more than the commute and you like having a true office/spare room, **Coburg** becomes more attractive despite ranking third.

## Quick Actions

Action: [Button: Pick South Yarra] https://www.ptv.vic.gov.au/
Action: [Button: Compare commute] https://www.google.com/maps

## Sources

- PTV Victoria trip planning and network info: <https://www.ptv.vic.gov.au/>
- Google Maps for door-to-door public transport timing: <https://www.google.com/maps>
- Consumer Affairs Victoria renting guidance: <https://www.consumer.vic.gov.au/housing/renting>

response_text:
## Best Fit for a Student in Manila

For a university student using about **18 GB/month**, **Plan Beta** is the best overall pick. It gives enough data headroom for daily messaging, maps, music streaming, and some hotspot use without pushing you into a much higher monthly cost.

Media: Icon=https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/bootstrap-icons@1.11.3/icons/phone.svg

## Plan Value and Usage Comparison

| Plan | Data | Calls/Texts | Hotspot | Monthly Price | Fit for 18 GB Use |
|---|---:|---|---|---:|---|
| Alpha | 15 GB | Unlimited | Not specified | ₱599 | Too tight; likely overage risk |
| Beta | 25 GB | Unlimited | 5 GB cap | ₱799 | Best balance of price and buffer |
| Gamma | 40 GB | Unlimited | No hotspot cap | ₱999 | Best for heavy hotspot or future growth |

### Why Beta wins
- **Enough data buffer:** At **18 GB usage**, Beta leaves about **7 GB spare** each month.
- **Better value than Gamma for typical student use:** You pay **₱200 less** than Gamma while still covering normal usage comfortably.
- **Lower overage risk than Alpha:** Alpha is **3 GB short** of your expected monthly use, so it is the most likely to trigger top-ups, throttling, or inconvenience.

### Value judgment
- **Alpha** only makes sense if your real usage often drops below **15 GB** and you are very price-sensitive.
- **Beta** is the sweet spot because it covers your needs without paying for a lot of unused data.
- **Gamma** is worth it only if you:
  - use hotspot regularly for laptop classes/work
  - expect your usage to rise above **25 GB**
  - want maximum flexibility and no hotspot cap concerns

## Student-Focused Recommendation

**Recommended plan: Plan Beta**

Why this is the most sensible choice in your case:
- Your usage is already above Alpha’s allowance.
- Manila mobile data use can climb fast with navigation, campus commuting, and streaming between Wi‑Fi zones.
- Occasional hotspot use fits within Beta’s **5 GB hotspot cap** for light backup use.
- The extra **₱200** for Gamma does **not** seem necessary unless hotspot becomes a frequent part of your routine.

## Quick Decision Guide

- Choose **Alpha** if saving money matters most and you can reliably stay under **15 GB**
- Choose **Beta** if you want the **best value with low stress**
- Choose **Gamma** if hotspot flexibility is important enough to justify paying more

## Context for This Recommendation

This assumes:
- your **18 GB/month** estimate is fairly consistent
- music streaming is moderate, not all-day high-bitrate use
- hotspot use is occasional, not a primary replacement for home or campus Wi‑Fi

If those assumptions hold, **Plan Beta is the best fit**.

response_text:
## Best Fit for a 3-Person Austin Household

For your priorities—**nut allergy safety first, vegetarian compatibility second, staying near a $95 weekly dinner budget third**—**Service B is the most practical overall pick**, with **Service A as the budget-friendly backup** only if the nut allergy is mild and you are comfortable with cross-contact risk.

## Service Comparison for Safety, Fit, and Budget

| Service | Weekly Plan Fit | Vegetarian Fit | Nut Allergy Caution | Budget Fit | Practicality for 3 | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Service A | 3 meals × 4 servings = 12 portions | Good; vegetarian options available | **Higher caution** due to possible cross-contamination warnings | **Within budget** at $89 | Good; leftovers from 4-serving meals | Good value, but weaker allergy safety |
| Service B | 4 meals × 3 servings = 12 portions | Moderate to good; customizable proteins may help vegetarian setup | **Moderate caution**; no peanut ingredients, but shared facility | Slightly over at $96 | **Best fit**; exact 3-serving dinners | Best overall balance |
| Service C | 10 prepared single portions | Possible, but less family-style | **Best labeling clarity** with clear allergen labels | **Over budget** at $110 | Less practical; not built for shared dinners | Safest labeling, but least practical |

Option 1: **Service B** | Best balance of portion fit, flexibility, and allergy management | **Most practical overall**
Action: [Button: Choose B] https://www.fda.gov/food/food-labeling-nutrition/food-allergies

Option 2: **Service A** | Best if strict budget matters most and allergy risk is manageable | **Lowest cost**
Action: [Button: Review allergy tips] https://www.foodallergy.org/resources/avoiding-cross-contact

Option 3: **Service C** | Best if allergen clarity matters more than budget and family-style meals | **Strongest labeling**
Action: [Button: Compare allergen labels] https://www.foodallergy.org/resources/how-read-food-label

## Recommended Choice and Allergy Cautions

### Recommended: Service B
Media: Icon=https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/bootstrap-icons@1.11.3/icons/shop.svg

Why it stands out:
- **Exact serving match** for a household of 3: 4 meals × 3 servings.
- **Very close to budget**: only $1 over your $95 target.
- **Customizable proteins** makes it easier to accommodate one vegetarian without fully splitting the meal plan.
- **No peanut ingredients** is stronger reassurance than Service A’s cross-contamination warning.

Allergy-related caution:
- A **shared facility** still means possible allergen cross-contact.
- “No peanut ingredients” does **not** guarantee tree-nut safety unless specifically stated.
- Best if you can verify:
  - whether tree nuts are used in the facility
  - whether dedicated lines/equipment are used
  - whether Austin-delivered meals have ingredient-level allergen filtering

### Budget Backup: Service A
Media: Icon=https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/bootstrap-icons@1.11.3/icons/currency-rupee.svg

Why it may work:
- **Under budget** at $89.
- Vegetarian options are clearly available.
- 4-serving meals can cover 3 people comfortably with one leftover portion.

Allergy-related caution:
- **Possible cross-contamination warnings** make this the **riskier choice** for a nut allergy household.
- If the allergy is severe or doctor-advised avoidance includes shared equipment/contact, this is **not the safest option**.

### Safety-First Alternative: Service C
Media: Icon=https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/bootstrap-icons@1.11.3/icons/shield-check.svg

Why it may appeal:
- **Clear allergen labels** are the strongest safety feature in the group.
- Prepared meals reduce ingredient ambiguity.

Trade-offs:
- **Over budget** at $110.
- **Less family-style**, so it is less convenient for shared dinners for 3.
- 10 single portions may not map neatly to a full week of household dinners.

## Quick Actions

Action: [Button: Food allergy guidance] https://www.foodallergy.org/
Action: [Button: FDA allergen info] https://www.fda.gov/food/food-labeling-nutrition/food-allergies

## Decision Context

I prioritized:
- **1. Allergy risk**
- **2. Vegetarian compatibility**
- **3. Staying at or near $95**
- **4. Ease of feeding exactly 3 people**

On that basis, **Service B wins on overall practicality**, while **Service C wins on labeling clarity** and **Service A wins on price**.

## Sources

- Food Allergy Research & Education: <https://www.foodallergy.org/resources/avoiding-cross-contact>
- FDA Food Allergies Overview: <https://www.fda.gov/food/food-labeling-nutrition/food-allergies>
- Reading Food Labels for Allergies: <https://www.foodallergy.org/resources/how-read-food-label>

response_text:
## UX Career Switch Fit

For your goals—**portfolio first**, **entry-level UX roles in London**, **8 hours/week**, **5 months**, **budget under $600**—the strongest path is:

**Best overall path: Course 2 → selected Course 1 modules/projects**
Media: Icon=https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/bootstrap-icons@1.11.3/icons/laptop.svg

Why this wins:
- **Course 2** gives the fastest portfolio output, which matters most for junior job applications.
- **Course 1** adds UX process credibility and research depth that many UI-only bootcamps lack.
- This combination can fit your **time** and **budget** if you use Course 1 selectively rather than completing the full certificate.

## Course Comparison for Your Constraints

| Option | Cost | Time Fit for 5 Months | Portfolio Value | UX Research Depth | Best Use |
|---|---:|---|---|---|---|
| Google UX certificate | $49/month | Moderate | Good | Strong | Structured UX foundations and case studies |
| UI design bootcamp | $499 one-time | Strong | Very strong | Limited | Fast portfolio building and visual execution |
| HCI university extension | $420 | Strong | Moderate | Strong | Theory, interaction principles, academic grounding |

## Recommended Learning Path

### Option 1: UI Bootcamp + Targeted Google UX Work
**Recommended choice**
Media: Icon=https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/bootstrap-icons@1.11.3/icons/star.svg

- Start with the **UI design bootcamp** to produce polished screens and portfolio-ready project work quickly.
- Add **1-2 months of Google UX certificate** for research methods, user journeys, wireframing, usability testing, and case-study framing.
- Skip the HCI extension unless you want deeper academic theory later.

**Why it fits best**
- Total likely cost: **about $597** ($499 + 2 months at $49)
- Total duration: **about 18-20 weeks**, matching your 5-month window
- Best balance of:
  - visual portfolio quality
  - enough UX process knowledge
  - realistic completion with 8 hours/week

### Option 2: Google UX Certificate Only
- Good if you want a more complete end-to-end UX process foundation.
- Less ideal for your situation because the estimated pace is **6 months**, and many learners need extra time to create polished portfolio pieces.
- It is affordable, but may leave you with **weaker visual presentation** unless you independently improve UI craft.

### Option 3: HCI Extension + Self-Directed Portfolio
- Useful for understanding design principles, usability, cognition, and interaction theory.
- Not the best primary route if the immediate goal is **job applications**.
- Employers hiring junior UX/UI candidates usually want to see **practical case studies**, not just theoretical understanding.

## 5-Month Portfolio-Focused Roadmap

| Phase | Goal | Key Tasks | Deliverable |
|---|---|---|---|
| Month 1 | Build core UI/UX momentum | Start UI bootcamp; learn Figma basics; choose 1 app problem space | First wireframes and visual system |
| Month 2 | Complete first strong project | Finish bootcamp project; refine flows; document decisions | Case study 1 |
| Month 3 | Add UX process depth | Start Google UX modules; user research; personas; journey map | Research-backed redesign project |
| Month 4 | Test and improve | Usability testing; iterate screens; improve information architecture | Case study 2 |
| Month 5 | Job application readiness | Build portfolio site/PDF; tailor CV; apply to London junior roles | 2 polished case studies + application pack |

## What to Build for London Entry-Level Roles

Aim to finish with:
- **2 strong case studies**
- **1 additional smaller visual/UI project**
- A portfolio showing:
  - problem framing
  - user research
  - wireframes
  - iteration
  - final UI
  - measurable reasoning for design decisions

Best project mix:
- **Case Study 1:** end-to-end product redesign from the UI bootcamp
- **Case Study 2:** research-led UX project from Google UX content
- **Mini Project:** landing page, dashboard, or mobile flow to show UI polish

This is better than trying to complete too many incomplete projects.

## Weekly Study Plan at 8 Hours

Media: Icon=https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/bootstrap-icons@1.11.3/icons/calendar.svg

A sustainable weekly split:
- **3 hours** course lessons
- **3 hours** project work in Figma
- **1 hour** portfolio writing
- **1 hour** job market review and inspiration

This keeps you producing visible work every week instead of only consuming course content.

## Best Final Recommendation

Choose:

**Primary path:** **Course 2 (UI design bootcamp)**
Then add
**Support path:** **2 months of Course 1 (Google UX certificate)**

Why this is the best decision in priority order:
1. **Portfolio building** — strongest with Course 2
2. **Entry-level job readiness** — stronger when paired with selected UX research/process work from Course 1
3. **Time limit** — realistic within 5 months at 8 hours/week
4. **Budget limit** — stays just under **$600**

Avoid making **Course 3** your main path for this transition. It is valuable academically, but it is the weakest match for your immediate hiring goal.

## Quick Actions

Action: [Button: Build Portfolio Brief] https://careerfoundry.com/en/blog/ux-design/ux-portfolio/
Action: [Button: Review London Roles] https://www.indeed.com/q-ux-designer-l-london-jobs.html

## Sources

- Google UX Design Certificate overview: <https://grow.google/certificates/ux-design/>
- Coursera pricing and certificate access: <https://www.coursera.org/professional-certificates/google-ux-design>
- UX portfolio guidance: <https://careerfoundry.com/en/blog/ux-design/ux-portfolio/>

response_text:
## Best Fit for a 900 sq ft, Low-Effort Cleaning Setup

For your priorities, **Option B robot vacuum is the best choice**. It fits your apartment size easily, handles pet hair and dust better, and requires the **least daily effort** thanks to mapping and the self-empty dock.

Context used:
- 900 sq ft apartment
- Mostly hardwood + 2 area rugs
- 1 cat
- Mild dust allergies
- Priority: **lowest day-to-day effort**

## Vacuum Choice Comparison

| Option | Price | Cleaning Fit | Daily Effort | Pet Hair/Dust | Best For |
|---|---:|---|---|---|---|
| Option A robot | $249 | Acceptable on hardwood; weaker on rugs | Low, but inconsistent | Fair | Budget automation |
| Option B robot | $399 | Strong on hardwood and rugs; mapped coverage | **Very low** | **Best** | Low-effort, allergy-aware cleaning |
| Cordless vacuum | $179 | Strong spot cleaning, fully manual | High | Good when used often | Lowest upfront cost |

### Why Option B wins
Media: Icon=https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/bootstrap-icons@1.11.3/icons/star.svg
- **Lidar mapping + room zoning** means it cleans methodically instead of wandering randomly.
- **5000 Pa suction** is much better for pulling cat hair and grit from rugs and edges.
- **Self-empty dock** reduces direct dust exposure, which matters for **mild allergies**.
- In a **900 sq ft apartment**, it should complete routine cleaning comfortably and keep floors consistently clean with almost no daily work.

### Where Option A falls short
Media: Icon=https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/bootstrap-icons@1.11.3/icons/signpost-split.svg
- **Random navigation** usually means more missed spots and longer cleaning sessions.
- **2000 Pa suction** is okay for light hardwood debris but less convincing for rug hair pickup.
- No mop and no dock means it saves some effort, but not nearly as much as Option B.

### Where the cordless vacuum still makes sense
Media: Icon=https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/bootstrap-icons@1.11.3/icons/lightning-charge.svg
- Best if your goal is **lowest purchase price**.
- Handy for furniture, corners, baseboards, and quick rug touch-ups.
- But it needs **you** to vacuum regularly, which conflicts with your “least daily effort” goal.

## Ranked Recommendation

Option 1: **Option B robot vacuum** | Best overall for automation, pet hair, and allergy-friendly upkeep | **Least daily effort**
Action: [Button: Choose Option B] https://www.irobot.com/

Option 2: **Cordless vacuum** | Best budget choice if you do not mind manual cleaning | **Lowest upfront cost**
Action: [Button: View Cordless Types] https://www.dyson.com/

Option 3: **Option A robot vacuum** | Entry-level automation, but weaker navigation and pickup | **Budget robot**
Action: [Button: Compare Robot Features] https://www.ecovacs.com/

## What This Means in Real Use

With your floors and cat, the biggest benefit is not just suction power—it is **consistent automatic cleaning**. Option B will likely keep hardwood dust, tracked litter, and fur under control with far less effort than either Option A or the cordless vacuum.

A practical setup:
- Run Option B **daily or every other day**
- Use a simple handheld or broom occasionally for sofa, corners, and tight edges
- Empty/replace the dock bag on schedule to reduce dust contact

## Quick Actions

Action: [Button: Compare robot models] https://www.rtings.com/vacuum
Action: [Button: Check allergy cleaning tips] https://www.aafa.org/allergy-proof-your-home/

## Sources

- Rtings vacuum testing and comparisons: <https://www.rtings.com/vacuum>
- Asthma and Allergy Foundation of America home cleaning guidance: <https://www.aafa.org/allergy-proof-your-home/>

## California Deposit Dispute Snapshot

Based on the dates you gave, the key practical issue is whether the landlord complied with California’s **21-day security deposit rule** and whether the deductions are supported by normal wear-and-tear standards.
A tenant in this situation should prepare a tight evidence packet, verify the timeline, and send a calm written dispute asking for backup documents and return of any improper deductions.

## Evidence and Timeline Review Checklist

| Item | What to gather or check | Why it matters | Your scenario |
|---|---|---|---|
| Lease and deposit records | Lease, deposit receipt, move-out date proof, forwarding address notice | Confirms deposit amount, tenancy terms, and when the 21-day clock started | Lease ended **2026-05-31**; deposit **$1,800** |
| Move-in condition proof | Move-in photos, inspection sheet, emails/texts about unit condition at move-in | Helps show pre-existing wear or baseline condition | You have **move-in photos** |
| Move-out condition proof | Move-out video, final cleaning receipts, utility shutoff, key return proof | Shows condition when possession ended | You have **move-out video** |
| Pre-move-out inspection issue | Check whether landlord offered an initial inspection before move-out and gave chance to cure | California law generally requires offering this for many residential tenancies | You said **no inspection was offered** |
| 21-day accounting deadline | Count 21 calendar days from move-out/vacate date to mailing/delivery of itemized statement and any refund | Late or noncompliant accounting can strengthen dispute position | From **2026-05-31**, day 21 is **2026-06-21**; itemization sent **2026-06-25** |
| Deduction support | Itemized statement, invoices, receipts, vendor estimates, photos of alleged damage | Landlord should support deductions, especially larger ones | Claimed: **Cleaning $250**, **Paint touch-up $400** |
| Wear and tear vs damage | Note scuffs, minor nail holes, light cleaning, ordinary aging versus unusual damage | Tenants usually are not charged for ordinary wear and tear | You report **no major damage** |
| Communications file | Emails, texts, portal messages, letters, mailing envelopes | Creates a clean timeline and shows what was or was not provided | Keep all landlord messages together |

## Practical Preparation for the Dispute Letter

### Document packet to assemble
Media: Icon=https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/bootstrap-icons@1.11.3/icons/folder.svg
- Signed lease or rental agreement.
- Proof of the **$1,800** security deposit.
- Proof of move-out date and key return.
- Copy of the landlord’s **2026-06-25** itemized deduction notice.
- Move-in photos.
- Move-out video.
- Any cleaning receipts or evidence the unit was left reasonably clean.
- Any texts/emails showing no initial inspection was offered.
- Notes describing each claimed deduction and why you dispute it.
- A simple date timeline: tenancy end, move-out, statement date, any refund date, your dispute date.

### Timeline points to review closely
Media: Icon=https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/bootstrap-icons@1.11.3/icons/calendar.svg
- **Move-out / surrender date:** confirm the exact date possession ended.
- **21-day deadline:** if possession ended **2026-05-31**, the itemized statement/refund was generally due by **2026-06-21**.
- **Delivery method:** note whether the deduction list was mailed, emailed, or posted in a portal, and preserve the envelope or timestamp if possible.
- **Initial inspection offer:** note that no pre-move-out inspection was offered, if true.
- **Receipts/invoices:** check whether actual receipts or good-faith estimates were included for the **$250 cleaning** and **$400 paint touch-up**.
- **Paint charges:** review whether the claimed touch-up is really for tenant-caused damage rather than routine repainting or minor scuffs.
- **Cleaning charges:** compare the landlord’s claim against the move-out video and whether the unit was returned to roughly the same cleanliness level, minus ordinary use.

### Points that may help a tenant here
Media: Icon=https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/bootstrap-icons@1.11.3/icons/shield-check.svg
- A statement sent on **2026-06-25** appears **4 days after** the 21-day mark if the clock started on **2026-05-31**.
- Failure to offer a pre-move-out inspection can matter because it may have deprived the tenant of a chance to fix issues before charges were imposed.
- **Ordinary wear and tear** generally is not deductible.
- Cleaning and paint deductions are commonly disputed when the evidence shows only normal use and no unusual damage.
- Large or unsupported charges are easier to challenge if receipts, photos, and before/after evidence are weak.

## Neutral Written Dispute Letter Outline

Use a professional, factual tone. Keep it short and attach evidence.

### Suggested structure
Media: Icon=https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/bootstrap-icons@1.11.3/icons/file-earmark-text.svg
- **Your name and address**
- **Date**
- **Landlord/property manager name and address**
- **Subject line:** Dispute of Security Deposit Deductions for [rental address]

### Body outline
1. **Opening**
- State the rental address, tenancy end date, and deposit amount.
- State that you are disputing some or all of the deductions listed in the notice dated **2026-06-25**.

2. **Timeline statement**
- State the date you vacated/surrendered possession.
- Note that California law generally requires an itemized statement and any remaining deposit within **21 days** of move-out.
- If accurate, state that the notice appears to have been sent after that period.

3. **Inspection issue**
- State that you were not offered a pre-move-out inspection, if true.
- Note this deprived you of an opportunity to address alleged issues before charges were assessed.

4. **Deduction-by-deduction dispute**
- **Cleaning $250:** state the unit was left reasonably clean; reference move-out video and any cleaning receipts.
- **Paint touch-up $400:** state there was no major damage and that minor marks/scuffs appear consistent with ordinary wear and tear; reference move-in photos and move-out video.

5. **Request for support**
- Ask for:
  - Copies of receipts, invoices, or estimates
  - Photos supporting the claimed damage
  - An explanation of how the paint charge was calculated
  - Prompt return of the disputed amount

6. **Requested resolution**
- Ask that the improper deductions be reversed and the disputed balance be returned by a specific reasonable date, such as **10-14 days** from the letter date.

7. **Closing**
- State that you hope to resolve the matter informally and promptly.
- Sign with your name and include email/phone.

### Short sample wording
“Dear [Landlord/Manager],
I am writing to dispute the security deposit deductions listed in your notice dated 2026-06-25 for the property at [address]. My tenancy ended on 2026-05-31, and my security deposit was $1,800.

I dispute the $250 cleaning charge and the $400 paint touch-up charge. Based on the condition of the unit at move-out, including my move-out video, there was no major damage beyond ordinary wear and tear. I also have move-in photographs showing the prior condition of the unit. In addition, I was not offered a pre-move-out inspection.

Please provide copies of any receipts, invoices, estimates, and photographs supporting these deductions, and return the disputed portion of the deposit. Because California law generally requires an itemized statement and return of any remaining deposit within 21 days, please also clarify the date and method by which the accounting was sent.

I would appreciate resolution of this matter within 14 days.”

For a marketing department split across New York and London, the strongest choice is **Tool A** for the best balance of **fast adoption, campaign visibility, and manageable cost**. It supports the team’s core needs well—**campaign planning, approval tracking, and weekly status reporting**—without the training overhead of a more complex platform.

## Tool Comparison for Marketing Workflows

| Tool | Ease of Adoption | Reporting | Collaboration | Fit for Campaign Planning | Fit for Approval Tracking | Weekly Status Reporting | Team Cost / Month |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Tool A | High | Good | Good | Strong via kanban + timeline | Good with board stages and basic automations | Good | **$120** |
| Tool B | High | Limited | Strong for docs/wiki | Moderate | Moderate, but more manual | Weak | **$96** |
| Tool C | Medium-Low | Strong | Good | Strong | Strong | Strong | **$228** |

### Recommendation: Tool A

Media: Icon=https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/bootstrap-icons@1.11.3/icons/bar-chart.svg

- **Best:** Tool A and Tool B
- **Why Tool A edges ahead:** It is easier to understand visually for campaign operations than a docs-heavy or highly configurable system.

- **Best:** Tool C
- **Best practical balance:** Tool A
- **Why this matters:** Weekly status reporting is a stated requirement, so Tool B is at a disadvantage.

- **Best for written collaboration:** Tool B
- **Best for operational oversight:** Tool C

- **Approval tracking:** Tool A or C
- **Weekly status reporting:** Tool C first, Tool A second

Choose **Tool A**.

It is the best fit because it:
- meets all three core needs reasonably well,
- is easiest to roll out quickly,
- supports visual campaign management for a distributed marketing team,
- and keeps cost at a sensible level: **$120/month total** for 12 users.

Choose **Tool C** only if leadership needs more advanced dashboards, workload balancing, and automation sophistication badly enough to justify the **higher cost and adoption effort**.

response_text:
## Kitchen Drain Issue: Best-Fit Service Category

Your symptoms most closely match a **non-emergency kitchen waste/drain blockage diagnosis and clearance** callout.

Media: Icon=https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/bootstrap-icons@1.11.3/icons/wrench.svg

Most likely service category to request:
- **Blocked sink / blocked kitchen waste pipe**
- **Drain unblocking / waste pipe clearance**
- **Kitchen sink and dishwasher waste investigation**

This does **not** currently sound like a whole-house drainage emergency because:
- Bathroom drains are normal
- There is **no sewage smell**
- The issue is intermittent rather than total backup
- The gurgling is limited to the nearby dishwasher connection area

For quoting, ask for a **fixed-price diagnostic + basic clearance visit** rather than a vague “plumbing repair” callout.

## Likely Causes and What Visit to Book

### Most probable causes
- **Grease, fat, soap, and food buildup** in the kitchen waste line
  This is the most common cause of slow kitchen sink drainage.
- **Partial blockage near the trap or branch connection** shared with the dishwasher waste
  Gurgling often suggests restricted airflow or water struggling past a partial clog.
- **Blocked or poorly venting standpipe/waste arrangement**
  Less likely, but possible if the dishwasher branch gulps air when the sink drains.
- **Small-scale issue in the external gully serving the kitchen**
  Possible if the kitchen line exits separately before joining the main drain.

### Less likely based on your description
- **Main sewer blockage**
- **Collapsed drain**
- **Major stack issue affecting the whole townhouse**

### Best service visit to request
Ask for:
- **Kitchen sink waste blockage diagnosis and clearance**
- **Check trap, branch waste, dishwasher connection, and nearby external gully**
- **Quote separately for CCTV only if basic clearance does not resolve it**

That keeps the first visit aligned with your **under-£250 target** and avoids jumping straight to expensive drain survey work.

### How urgent it sounds
- **Priority: routine / soon, not emergency**
- Book within a few days if possible
- It becomes urgent if you get:
  - Water backing up into the sink or dishwasher
  - Multiple fixtures slowing at once
  - Bad odours
  - Overflow or leaking under the sink
  - No drainage at all

## Quote Comparison Checklist

| Check | What to ask | What to look for | Good sign |
|---|---|---|---|
| Service type | “Is this priced as kitchen waste blockage clearance?” | Specific scope, not generic plumbing | Clear mention of trap/waste/drain check |
| Pricing model | “Is this fixed price or callout plus hourly?” | Avoid open-ended labour unless necessary | Fixed first-hour or fixed blockage rate |
| Included work | “Does the price include trap removal, rodding, and basic machine clearing?” | Scope should match likely issue | Basic clearance included in base quote |
| Extra charges | “What triggers extra cost?” | Watch for vague add-ons | CCTV/parts only if needed and approved |
| External check | “Will you inspect the outside gully if relevant?” | Useful for kitchen-only recurring issues | Included or low-cost add-on |
| Evidence | “Will you explain what caused it and what was done?” | Helps compare quality, not just price | Before/after notes or photos |
| Guarantee | “Do you offer a short guarantee on blockage recurrence?” | Many offer limited blockage warranty | 14–90 day workmanship/clearance cover |
| Timing | “What is your earliest routine appointment?” | Emergency pricing may blow budget | Standard appointment slot available |

## What to Ask Plumbers Before You Book

Use this shortlist when calling or messaging:

- “I have a **slow-draining kitchen sink** with **occasional gurgling near the dishwasher waste**, but bathrooms are normal. Does this sound like a **kitchen waste blockage** visit?”
- “What is your **fixed price** for diagnosis and basic clearance?”
- “Does that include checking the **trap, dishwasher branch, and outside gully**?”
- “If you can’t clear it on the first visit, what would the **next-step cost** be?”
- “Do you use **rods, wet vac, or drain machine** for kitchen waste blockages?”
- “Would you recommend **CCTV only if the blockage recurs**?”
- “Are there any **evening/weekend surcharges**?”
- “Is VAT included in the quote?”
- “Do you provide a **written estimate or invoice** before extra work?”
- “Do you guarantee the clearance for any period?”

## Price Expectations for Your Budget

### Reasonable target in Glasgow for this issue
Media: Icon=https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/bootstrap-icons@1.11.3/icons/currency-pound.svg

For a routine, non-emergency kitchen blockage visit, a sensible quote range is often:
- **£80–£150** for straightforward internal waste blockage clearance
- **£120–£220** if external gully check or more involved clearance is needed
- **£200–£350+** if CCTV survey, repeat attendance, or more complex drain access is involved

### Best quote structure for you
Given your budget target, the best estimate format is:
- **Fixed callout with diagnosis**
- **Basic clearance included**
- **Any CCTV or parts pre-approved separately**

That helps keep the likely first visit **under £250** unless they find a more complex external or structural issue.

## Best Booking Wording to Use

When requesting quotes, send this:

“Kitchen sink in a 2-storey townhouse is draining slowly and there is occasional gurgling from the adjacent dishwasher drain. No sewage smell, bathrooms drain normally, issue has been on and off for 3 weeks. Looking for a **routine kitchen waste blockage diagnosis and clearance**, ideally **fixed price**, with check of trap, dishwasher connection, and nearby external gully if relevant. Budget target under **£250** unless urgent or a larger issue is found.”

## Quick Actions

Action: [Button: Compare quotes] https://www.mybuilder.com/plumbing/plumber-tradespeople/glasgow

## Sources

- UK consumer guidance on hiring trades: <https://www.citizensadvice.org.uk/consumer/get-more-help-if-youre-problem-with-a-builder-or-trader/>
- Trusted trader listings in Glasgow: <https://www.checkatrade.com/Search/plumbers/in/glasgow>
- Trade quote comparison platform: <https://www.mybuilder.com/plumbing/plumber-tradespeople/glasgow>

response_text:
## Monthly Budget Snapshot

Media: Icon=https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/bootstrap-icons@1.11.3/icons/currency-dollar.svg

- **Net income:** $4,200
- **Current total spending:** $3,953
- **Current leftover:** **$247**
- **Target extra freed up:** **$350/month**
- **Retirement kept unchanged:** **$400/month**

You do not need to cut essentials aggressively to hit the goal. The easiest path is trimming flexible categories first: dining out, miscellaneous, groceries, subscriptions, and the travel fund.

## Prioritized Spending Cuts

Formula: Freed cash = sum of category reductions

| Category | Current | Recommended | Cut | Why this is a good cut |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| Dining out | $340 | $190 | **$150** | Biggest easy-win; still leaves room for occasional meals out |
| Miscellaneous | $310 | $210 | **$100** | Often absorbs impulse spending and untracked purchases |
| Groceries | $520 | $470 | **$50** | Moderate trim via meal planning, store brands, fewer convenience items |
| Subscriptions | $78 | $38 | **$40** | Cancel/pause low-use services first |
| Travel sinking fund | $250 | $200 | **$50** | Preserves travel savings while freeing cash now |

- **Total recommended cuts:** **$390/month**
- This beats your **$350** target without touching retirement.
- New leftover after cuts: **$637/month** total cushion, which is **$390 more than before**.

## Revised Monthly Budget

| Category | Current | Revised |
|---|---:|---:|
| Net income | $4,200 | $4,200 |
| Rent | $1,450 | $1,450 |
| Utilities | $180 | $180 |
| Groceries | $520 | $470 |
| Dining out | $340 | $190 |
| Transportation | $260 | $260 |
| Phone | $65 | $65 |
| Internet | $55 | $55 |
| Subscriptions | $78 | $38 |
| Gym | $45 | $45 |
| Travel sinking fund | $250 | $200 |
| Retirement | $400 | $400 |
| Miscellaneous | $310 | $210 |
| **Total spending** | **$3,953** | **$3,563** |
| **Left over** | **$247** | **$637** |

## Best Cut Plan for the Least Pain

Option 1: Cut flexible lifestyle spending first | Frees the full target with minimal disruption to fixed bills | **Best overall**
- Dining out: -$150
- Miscellaneous: -$100
- Groceries: -$50
- Subscriptions: -$40
- Travel fund: -$50

Option 2: Protect travel more | If travel matters a lot, keep that at $250 and cut a bit more elsewhere | **Good alternative**
- Dining out: -$160
- Miscellaneous: -$120
- Groceries: -$60
- Subscriptions: -$50
- Total freed: **$390**

Option 3: More balanced but stricter | Smaller cuts across more categories | **Works, but harder to sustain**
- Groceries: -$70
- Dining out: -$120
- Transportation: -$30
- Subscriptions: -$40
- Miscellaneous: -$80
- Travel fund: -$30
- Total freed: **$370**

## Practical Ways to Make the Cuts Stick

- **Dining out:** set a weekly cap of about **$45**.
- **Groceries:** plan 2 cheap repeat dinners each week; switch some name brands to store brands.
- **Miscellaneous:** give yourself a fixed monthly “fun money” cap and stop once it’s gone.
- **Subscriptions:** review every recurring charge and keep only the 1–2 most used.
- **Travel fund:** temporarily reduce, not eliminate, until your monthly cushion feels strong.

## Quick Actions

Action: [Button: Budget tracker] https://www.consumer.gov/managing-your-money/making-budget
Action: [Button: Spending worksheet] https://www.ramseysolutions.com/budgeting/budget-template

## Sources

- Consumer budgeting guidance: <https://www.consumer.gov/managing-your-money/making-budget>
- CFPB budgeting resources: <https://www.consumerfinance.gov/consumer-tools/budgeting/>
- Monthly budget worksheet reference: <https://www.fdic.gov/resources/consumers/money-smart/>

response_text:
## Two-Week Fatigue: Likely Non-Emergency Causes
Media: Icon=https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/bootstrap-icons@1.11.3/icons/thermometer-half.svg

For a generally healthy 34-year-old office worker, **two weeks of tiredness** is often related to common, non-urgent factors rather than a serious illness. This is informational only and not a diagnosis.

A few plausible causes:
- **Poor sleep quality**: inconsistent bedtime, screen time, snoring, late caffeine, or stress-disrupted sleep
- **Workload and stress**: mental fatigue, burnout, prolonged concentration, or not enough recovery time
- **Seasonal allergies**: allergy symptoms themselves, poor sleep from congestion, or sedating antihistamines
- **Tension headaches**: pain, muscle tightness, dehydration, and poor posture can all leave you drained
- **Dehydration or irregular meals**: not drinking enough water, skipping meals, or relying on caffeine/sugar swings
- **Low physical activity**: long desk hours can worsen sluggishness and stiffness
- **Recent mild viral illness**: even a minor cold can leave temporary fatigue afterward
- **Mood factors**: low mood, anxiety, irritability, or emotional strain can show up mainly as tiredness

## Reasonable Self-Care for the Next Several Days

| Area | What to try | Why it may help | Reasonable timeframe |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sleep | Aim for 7-9 hours; consistent sleep/wake time; limit screens 1 hour before bed | Improves sleep depth and recovery | 3-7 days |
| Allergies | Reduce exposure; consider non-drowsy allergy strategies already known to work for you; avoid sedating meds if possible | Less congestion and less medication-related drowsiness | 2-5 days |
| Hydration | Drink water regularly through the day; reduce excess alcohol | Dehydration commonly causes fatigue and headaches | 1-3 days |
| Food | Eat regular meals with protein, fiber, fruit/veg; avoid long gaps without eating | Prevents energy dips | 2-5 days |
| Activity | Add light daily movement: 10-20 minute walks, stretch breaks, posture changes | Helps circulation, alertness, and tension headaches | Same day to 1 week |
| Headache care | Gentle neck/shoulder stretches, screen breaks, ergonomic adjustments, hydration | Reduces muscle-tension-related fatigue | 1-3 days |
| Caffeine | Keep caffeine moderate and avoid it late in the day | Can improve energy without worsening sleep | 2-4 days |
| Stress reset | Short breaks, lighter evenings, breathing exercises, or one lower-demand weekend day | Mental fatigue improves with recovery time | Several days |

## When a Doctor Visit Becomes Reasonable
Media: Icon=https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/bootstrap-icons@1.11.3/icons/calendar.svg

Booking a **non-urgent doctor visit** is reasonable if:
- tiredness lasts **more than 2-4 weeks**
- fatigue is **getting worse** instead of improving
- it starts interfering with **work, exercise, or daily tasks**
- you are sleeping enough but still wake feeling unrefreshed
- headaches become **more frequent, more intense, or different than usual**
- allergy symptoms are severe or treatment seems to make you unusually sleepy
- you notice **low mood, anxiety, poor concentration, or loss of interest** persisting alongside the fatigue
- you have recurrent fatigue with no clear trigger

## Warning Signs That Should Not Be Ignored

Seek prompt medical evaluation sooner if fatigue comes with:
- **shortness of breath**
- **chest pain**
- **fainting** or near-fainting
- **new confusion**
- **high fever**
- **unexplained weight loss**
- **persistent vomiting**
- **blood in stool**, black stools, or unusual bleeding
- **marked weakness**, numbness, or trouble speaking
- a **sudden severe headache** or a clearly unusual headache pattern
- significant swelling, palpitations, or symptoms that feel rapidly worsening

## Practical Next Steps
- Track for 5-7 days: sleep hours, allergy symptoms, headaches, hydration, caffeine, and energy level.
- Review whether an allergy medicine or recent routine change matches the timing.
- If fatigue is still present after a solid week of self-care, **booking a routine doctor visit is reasonable**.

## Sources
- - NHS fatigue overview: <https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/tiredness-and-fatigue/>
- - MedlinePlus on fatigue: <https://medlineplus.gov/fatigue.html>
- - Mayo Clinic healthy sleep tips: <https://www.mayoclinic.org/healthy-lifestyle/adult-health/in-depth/sleep/art-20048379>

## Best Laptops for a CS Student Under $1,200

All three options meet your hard requirements: **under $1,200**, **16GB RAM**, and **512GB SSD**.
Prioritizing **battery life**, **portability**, and **coding performance** over gaming, the best overall pick is the **Acer Swift Go 14**.

## Ranked Laptop Comparison

| Rank | Laptop | Price | Weight | Battery | CPU | Why it ranks here |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---|---|
| 1 | Acer Swift Go 14 | $899 | 1.3 kg | 12 hrs | Intel Core Ultra 5 | Best balance of battery, lowest weight, and strong everyday coding value |
| 2 | ASUS Zenbook 14 OLED | $1,099 | 1.39 kg | 10 hrs | Ryzen 7 7840U | Strongest raw performance, premium feel, but shorter battery and higher price |
| 3 | Lenovo IdeaPad Slim 5 14 | $749 | 1.46 kg | 11 hrs | Ryzen 5 7540U | Best budget value, but heaviest and slightly weaker for heavier dev workloads |

Option 1: **Acer Swift Go 14** | Best overall for student use with the longest battery life and lightest chassis | **Top balance**
Media: Icon=https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/bootstrap-icons@1.11.3/icons/laptop.svg
- Best fit for carrying to class every day.
- 12-hour battery is the best here, which matters more than small CPU gains for most CS workflows.
- Core Ultra 5 is easily enough for coding, browser tabs, IDEs, Docker/light VMs, and coursework.
- At $899, it leaves room in budget for accessories like a monitor, mouse, or external SSD.

Option 2: **ASUS Zenbook 14 OLED** | Best performance choice if you want extra CPU headroom and a nicer display | **Fastest CPU**
Media: Icon=https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/bootstrap-icons@1.11.3/icons/laptop.svg
- Ryzen 7 7840U is the strongest processor of the three for heavier compiling, multitasking, and more demanding dev tools.
- Still portable, but battery life is the weakest here at 10 hours.
- Costs $200 more than the Acer for performance you may not fully notice in typical student coding use.
- Best trade-off only if you value extra speed more than battery/runtime.

Option 3: **Lenovo IdeaPad Slim 5 14** | Best low-cost pick with solid specs, but less refined for your priorities | **Best budget**
Media: Icon=https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/bootstrap-icons@1.11.3/icons/laptop.svg
- Cheapest by a wide margin and still meets the 16GB requirement.
- Ryzen 5 7540U is good for programming, coursework, and daily productivity.
- Slightly heavier than both rivals, so it is less ideal if portability is a top priority.
- Good value, but it gives up some comfort and performance polish versus the top two.

## Trade-Offs That Matter Most

### Battery life and portability
- **Acer Swift Go 14** wins clearly: lightest at **1.3 kg** and longest battery at **12 hours**.
- **ASUS Zenbook 14 OLED** is still portable, but **10 hours** is the shortest runtime here.
- **Lenovo IdeaPad Slim 5 14** is acceptable, but **1.46 kg** is the least travel-friendly.

### Coding performance
- **ASUS Zenbook 14 OLED** has the best CPU for heavier workloads like larger codebases, more containers, and sustained multitasking.
- **Acer Swift Go 14** should still feel very strong for most CS student needs: VS Code/JetBrains, Python, Java, web dev, and moderate local development tools.
- **Lenovo IdeaPad Slim 5 14** is competent, but the least powerful of the three.

### Value for money
- **Lenovo IdeaPad Slim 5 14** gives the lowest price and still checks all the basics.
- **Acer Swift Go 14** offers the best value-to-usability mix for your stated priorities.
- **ASUS Zenbook 14 OLED** is the premium choice, but the extra spend mainly buys performance, not battery.

## Final Recommendation for a CS Student

**1) Acer Swift Go 14 — Best overall choice**
If your priority order is really **battery life first, portability second, coding performance third**, this is the smartest buy.

**2) ASUS Zenbook 14 OLED — Best performance upgrade**
Choose this only if you expect heavier dev workloads and are okay paying more for less battery.

**3) Lenovo IdeaPad Slim 5 14 — Best budget fallback**
Pick this if saving money matters most and you can accept a bit more weight and less performance.

Under $1,200

All three options meet your hard requirements. Prioritizing battery life, portability, and coding performance over gaming, the best overall pick is the Acer Swift Go 14.
Ranked Laptop Comparison
Top Options
Option 1: Acer Swift Go 14

Best overall for student use with the longest battery life and lightest chassis. Best fit for carrying to class every day. The 12-hour battery matters more than small CPU gains for most CS workflows. Core Ultra 5 is easily enough for coding, browser tabs, IDEs, Docker, light virtual machines, and coursework. At $899, it leaves room in budget for accessories like a monitor, mouse, or external SSD.
Option 2: ASUS Zenbook 14 OLED

Best performance choice if you want extra CPU headroom and a nicer display. Ryzen 7 7840U is the strongest processor of the three for heavier compiling, multitasking, and more demanding development tools. It is still portable, but battery life is the weakest here at 10 hours. It costs $200 more than the Acer for performance you may not fully notice in typical student coding use.
Option 3: Lenovo IdeaPad Slim 5 14

Best low-cost pick with solid specs, but less refined for your priorities. It is the cheapest by a wide margin and still meets the 16GB requirement. Ryzen 5 7540U is good for programming, coursework, and daily productivity. It is slightly heavier than both rivals, so it is less ideal if portability is a top priority.
Trade-Offs That Matter Most
Final Recommendation for a CS Student
1. Acer Swift Go 14 — Best overall choice. If your priority order is battery life first, portability second, and coding performance third, this is the smartest buy.
2. ASUS Zenbook 14 OLED — Best performance upgrade. Choose this only if you expect heavier development workloads and are okay paying more for less battery.
3. Lenovo IdeaPad Slim 5 14 — Best budget fallback. Pick this if saving money matters most and you can accept a bit more weight and less performance.

response_text:
## Ontario Lease Exit: What to Review First

Media: Icon=https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/bootstrap-icons@1.11.3/icons/house.svg

This is an informational checklist for an Ontario residential tenant on a 12-month lease starting **2025-09-01** who wants to leave after about 3 months due to relocation. In Ontario, a landlord usually cannot simply insist on collecting all remaining rent automatically without trying to reduce losses, and the tenant may have options such as **assignment, sublet, agreed termination, or negotiated repayment**.

## Lease-End Options and Review Checklist

| Option | What to Review | Key Benefit | Main Risk/Limit |
|---|---|---|---|
| Assignment | Does the lease restrict assignment; has the tenant asked for landlord consent in writing | Can transfer the lease and often end ongoing responsibility if properly completed | Requires landlord involvement and a suitable replacement |
| Sublet | Whether temporary absence fits a sublet and whether tenant plans to return before lease end | Useful if the tenant expects to come back before the term ends | Original tenant usually remains responsible to landlord |
| Mutual termination | Whether landlord will sign an N11 or other written end-of-tenancy agreement | Cleanest exit if both sides agree | Landlord may ask for compensation |
| Negotiation | Whether landlord will accept a fixed payment, forfeited deposit treatment where lawful, or shorter liability period | May reduce conflict and cap cost quickly | Must be documented clearly in writing |
| Early move-out without agreement | Whether landlord can re-rent quickly and what proof exists of re-rental efforts | May pressure practical resolution if market is strong | Highest dispute risk; landlord may claim rent losses and costs |

## Questions and Documents to Prepare

### What the tenant should review in the lease
- The exact **term dates**: 2025-09-01 to 2026-08-31.
- Any clause about **assignment, subletting, or early termination**.
- Notice requirements for asking to assign or sublet.
- Any clause claiming the tenant owes **all remaining rent automatically**; such wording may not be enforceable if inconsistent with Ontario law.
- Whether there are separate charges for advertising, key replacement, cleaning, or re-rental.

### What to gather before replying
- A copy of the signed lease.
- Proof of the **job relocation** if helpful for negotiation.
- A draft move-out date.
- Payment history and current rent balance.
- Copies of all texts/emails with the landlord.
- Evidence of potential replacement tenants, if available.

### Key questions to ask the landlord
- Will you agree to an **assignment** of the lease if I find a qualified replacement?
- If not, will you give that refusal **in writing**?
- Will you agree to a **mutual termination** on a specific date?
- If you claim rent after move-out, what steps will you take to **re-rent the unit promptly**?
- Are you asking for actual losses only, or the entire remaining rent regardless of re-rental?
- What documentation will you provide for any claimed losses or costs?
- If I propose a replacement tenant, what screening criteria will you use?

### Key questions the tenant should ask themselves
- Do I want a **clean break** now, or can I help line up a replacement?
- Am I leaving permanently, or is a **sublet** more appropriate?
- Is the rental market strong enough that the unit may re-rent quickly?
- Would a modest negotiated payment be cheaper than a prolonged dispute?

## Practical Response Path Before Answering the Landlord

Option 1: **Request assignment approval in writing** | Best first step if the tenant wants to minimize liability and leave properly | Often strongest practical option
Action: [Button: Request Assignment] https://tribunalsontario.ca/ltb/help-for-tenants/

Option 2: **Propose a mutual termination date** | Best for a clean documented exit if the landlord is cooperative | Use a signed written agreement only
Action: [Button: Review N11 Info] https://tribunalsontario.ca/ltb/forms/

Option 3: **Negotiate a capped settlement** | Useful if the landlord resists assignment but may accept a shorter payment period | Get exact amount and release terms in writing
Action: [Button: Get Legal Info] https://stepstojustice.ca/legal-topic/housing-law/

Option 4: **Do not accept “full remaining rent no matter what” at face value** | The landlord may need to justify actual losses and efforts to re-rent | Disputes may go to the Landlord and Tenant Board
Action: [Button: LTB Information] https://tribunalsontario.ca/ltb/

## Best Next Moves Before Responding

- Reply in writing, calmly and briefly.
- Ask for consent to **assign** the tenancy or for a **mutual termination**.
- Do not agree that you owe the entire remaining term automatically unless you have reviewed the consequences.
- Ask the landlord to confirm, in writing, whether they will try to re-rent and how they will calculate any claimed loss.
- Keep every communication and avoid phone-only discussions for anything important.

## Sources

- LTB main information page: <https://tribunalsontario.ca/ltb/>
- LTB forms and notices: <https://tribunalsontario.ca/ltb/forms/>
- Steps to Justice housing law guides: <https://stepstojustice.ca/legal-topic/housing-law/>

response_text:
## 2016 Civic Cold-Start Squeal: Most Likely Causes
Your symptoms point most strongly to a **serpentine belt or belt tensioner issue**, not a battery problem. A brief squeal only on cold start, with **normal driving, no warning lights, and no headlight dimming**, usually means the belt slips for a moment until it warms up and grips.

Media: Icon=https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/bootstrap-icons@1.11.3/icons/car-front.svg

Most likely causes, in order:
- **Worn serpentine belt** — glazed, hardened, slightly stretched, or cracked belt can squeal briefly when cold.
- **Weak automatic belt tensioner** — if spring tension is low, the belt can slip at startup.
- **Pulley bearing beginning to wear** — idler, tensioner pulley, alternator pulley, or A/C compressor pulley can chirp/squeal.
- **Minor moisture/contamination on belt** — less likely if it happens regularly, but possible.
- **Alternator drag on startup** — possible, but less likely given no dimming or battery warning signs.

## Mechanic Checks to Request
Ask for a **belt-drive inspection first**, since it is the cheapest and most likely path.

| Step | Action | What to Check | Expected Result |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Inspect serpentine belt | Cracks, glazing, frayed edges, contamination, hardness | Belt condition clearly pass/fail |
| 2 | Check belt tensioner | Weak spring, poor damping, arm movement, alignment | Tensioner holds steady tension |
| 3 | Spin pulleys by hand | Roughness, wobble, noise in idler/tensioner/accessory pulleys | Pulleys spin smoothly and quietly |
| 4 | Check belt alignment | Misaligned pulleys or belt tracking off-center | Belt tracks straight |
| 5 | Cold-start listen test | Source of squeal during first few seconds | Noise isolated to specific pulley/belt area |
| 6 | Charging-system test | Alternator output and battery voltage under load | Normal charging, no overload signs |

What to specifically say:
- “Please inspect the **serpentine belt, tensioner, idler pulleys, and alternator pulley** for a cold-start squeal.”
- “If possible, do a **cold-start diagnosis before replacing parts**.”
- “Please quote me **belt only** versus **belt + tensioner** so I can stay under budget.”

Typical cost range:
- **Belt only:** about **$120–$220**
- **Belt + tensioner:** about **$250–$450**
- **Add pulley/idler if needed:** often **$80–$200** more
- This usually fits your **$600 budget** unless multiple pulleys/accessories are failing.

## Urgent vs Safe to Monitor Briefly
### Address soon
- **Serpentine belt wear**
- **Weak belt tensioner**
- **Noisy idler/tensioner pulley**

These are not usually “stop driving today” problems if the noise is brief and the car is otherwise normal, but they **should be handled soon**, especially with a daily 25-mile commute. If the belt system fails, you can lose:
- Alternator charging
- Water pump function on some setups
- Power steering assist on belt-driven systems
- A/C

### Usually okay to monitor for a short time
If all of these remain true, brief monitoring is reasonable for **a few days to a couple of weeks max** while scheduling service:
- Squeal lasts only a few seconds
- Only occurs on cold starts
- No burning smell
- No battery/charging warning light
- No overheating
- No steering change
- No worsening noise while driving

### Treat as urgent immediately
Do **not** keep monitoring if any of these appear:
- Squeal becomes **louder or longer**
- Noise happens **while driving**, not just at startup
- **Battery light** comes on
- **Engine temperature rises**
- Belt area shows **visible wobble**
- You hear **grinding**, not just squealing
- You notice **rubber dust**, fraying, or a loose belt

## Best Fit for Your Budget and Commute
For your mileage and symptoms, the smartest plan is:

Option 1: Inspect and likely replace serpentine belt | Most common fix for short cold-start squeal | Lowest-cost starting point
Action: [Button: Find Honda Service] https://automobiles.honda.com/tools/dealership-locator

Option 2: Replace belt and tensioner together if tension is weak | Best value if original parts are still on the car at 92k miles | Stronger long-term reliability
Action: [Button: Get Repair Estimate] https://repairpal.com/estimator

Option 3: Add pulley replacement only if noise is isolated there | Avoids unnecessary parts swapping | Keeps total under control
Action: [Button: Compare Fair Price] https://www.kbb.com/auto-repair/

## Quick Actions
Action: [Button: Book Inspection] https://automobiles.honda.com/tools/dealership-locator
Action: [Button: Check Repair Cost] https://repairpal.com/estimator

## Sources
- Honda dealer locator: <https://automobiles.honda.com/tools/dealership-locator>
- RepairPal estimator: <https://repairpal.com/estimator>
- Kelley Blue Book repair pricing: <https://www.kbb.com/auto-repair/>

## Best Choice for Your Priorities

**Recommended: Plan B — 150 Mbps at £39/month**

Media: Icon=https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/bootstrap-icons@1.11.3/icons/wifi.svg

- **Why it wins:** It balances **price, speed, and household stability** better than the others.
- **Why 150 Mbps matters:** It gives comfortable room for:
  - 2 simultaneous video meetings
  - online gaming with low congestion risk
  - background cloud sync, software updates, and streaming
- **Why not Plan A:** 63 Mbps is not terrible, but in a busy home it can become the kind of connection that is “fine until everyone is online at once.”
- **Why not Plan D:** 35 Mbps is the cheapest, but it is the most likely to cause friction for work calls, downloads, and shared use.
- **Why not Plan C:** 500 Mbps is excellent, but at **£46** it misses your budget cap. If that £1 matters, it drops behind Plan B.

## When Paying More Is Worth It

Paying more is worth it when the extra cost clearly reduces real household pain:

- **Choose Plan B over Plan A** if:
  - both adults are often on video calls at the same time
  - the teenager games while others stream or work
  - you want fewer slowdowns during evening peak use
  For **£11 more per month**, Plan B buys a much safer performance margin.

- **Choose Plan C over Plan B** if:
  - your budget can stretch slightly above £45
  - you do large cloud backups, frequent big downloads, or 4K streaming on multiple screens
  - you value the **shorter 12-month contract**
  In that case, the extra speed is less about basic usability and more about convenience, faster downloads, and future-proofing.

- **Choose Plan D over others** only if:
  - flexibility matters more than speed
  - you may move soon or dislike long contracts
  The rolling term is useful, but this is the weakest fit for your usage.
